FUTURE_pre: It has made me realize I wanted to stay in the academy. Not necessarily as a tenure-track professor with a lab at an R1, but as a research scientist / lecturer / educational design instructor. Initially I didn't want to do industry or academia (I wanted to work in the federal govt) but now I am more amenable to roles where I mentor undergrads and work with improving opportunities for underrepresented folks in STEM
FUTURE_post: I realized I like mentoring undergrads in research but only when the structure is outlined / there’s a clear game plan to follow. Like, for example, our hub was in its first year so it was really hard to design a new research program from the ground up and mentor students.

FUTURE_pre: I love mentoring undergraduate research and hope to be able to continue doing so by working at a student- and service-oriented liberal arts college

It has definitely reinforced the idea that there needs to be better faculty mentors that understand students’ ethnic backgrounds or at least are attentive to it, especially when doing research in the social sciences. As a result, I’ve been inspired to continue pursuing an academic career.
My experiences mentoring undergraduates in research have made me realize how much I truly enjoy teaching. It has strengthened my desire to pursue a career that combines research and teaching...

It made me aware of how I could try to build out larger research initiatives as opposed to individual, discrete research projects. My actual career plans have not changed much, since I wanted to be a professor any way, but I've been more considerate of what resources, centers, opportunities, etc. that I want to search for when joining a University.
Mentoring undergraduates has strengthened my enthusiasm for pursuing a career in academia, as it allows me to cultivate teaching skills, share knowledge, and witness students’ growth firsthand.
It made me see myself as more of a manager which can certainly open up ideas for my career options.
FUTURE_post: I think this experience didn’t change my career interests but definitely reinforced and confirmed my desire to want to work as a part of multidisciplinary teams. I really liked having people from molecular biology, mechanical engineering, cs, etc.

FUTURE_pre: It has encouraged me to stay in academia where I can do research while maintaining a teaching / mentorship role

FUTURE_post: I greatly enjoyed this experience and look forward to mentoring more students in the future! I learned a great deal about how to motivate undergraduates in a hypothesis-driven manner while encouraging consistent collection of high quality data. Having to manage other researchers forced me to think critically about medium- and long-term project management in ways that made me more responsible for my own project and potential side projects. The experience has taught me a great deal about mentorship and encouraged me to vigorously consider an academic career.
I knew I wanted to teach, but I hadn’t considered teaching research methods before. But I had such a good experience with my mentees that now I would happily teach methods.

The experience has certainly nourished my interest in teaching writ large -- a viable career pathway at multiple levels. Somewhat more melancholically, though, it's also shown me just how good TT faculty at R1s and SLACs have it, since this is the kind of work they get to do with undergraduates and graduate students on a regular basis!

Mentoring students through the CICI Discovery Program this year was invaluable. I feel much more confident in entering the academic job market now that I can speak to specific ways I mentor undergraduates.
